{{Short description|Function made from a set}}
[[File:Minkowski functional.svg|thumb]]

In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[functional analysis]], a '''Minkowski functional''' (after [[Hermann Minkowski]]) or '''gauge function''' is a function that recovers a notion of distance on a linear space.

If <math display="inline">K</math> is a subset of a [[Real number|real]] or [[Complex number|complex]] [[vector space]] <math display="inline">X,</math> then the {{em|Minkowski functional}} or {{em|gauge}} of <math display="inline">K</math> is defined to be the [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math display="inline">p_K : X \to [0, \infty],</math> valued in the [[Extended real number line|extended real number]]s, defined by
<math display=block>p_K(x) = \inf \{r \in \R : r > 0 \text{ and } x \in r K\}, \quad  x \in X,</math>
where the [[Infimum and supremum|infimum]] of the empty set is defined to be [[positive infinity]].

The set <math display="inline">K</math> is often assumed to have properties, such as being an [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] in <math display="inline">X</math>, that guarantee that <math display="inline">p_K</math> will be a [[seminorm]] on <math display="inline">X.</math> In fact, every seminorm <math display="inline">p</math> on <math display="inline">X</math> is equal to the Minkowski functional (that is, <math display="inline">p = p_K</math>) of any subset <math display="inline">K</math> of <math display="inline">X</math> satisfying

<math display="block">\{x \in X : p(x) < 1\} \subseteq K \subseteq \{x \in X : p(x) \leq 1\}</math>

(where all three of these sets are necessarily absorbing in <math display="inline">X</math> and the first and last are also disks).

Thus every seminorm (which is a {{em|function}} defined by purely algebraic properties) can be associated (non-uniquely) with an absorbing disk (which is a {{em|set}} with certain geometric properties) and conversely, every absorbing disk can be associated with its Minkowski functional (which will necessarily be a seminorm). 
These relationships between seminorms, Minkowski functionals, and absorbing disks is a major reason why Minkowski functionals are studied and used in functional analysis. 
In particular, through these relationships, Minkowski functionals allow one to "translate" certain {{em|geometric}} properties of a subset of <math display="inline">X</math> into certain {{em|algebraic}} properties of a function on <math display="inline">X.</math>

The Minkowski function is always non-negative (meaning <math display="inline">p_K \geq 0</math>). 
This property of being nonnegative stands in contrast to other classes of functions, such as [[sublinear function]]s and real [[linear functionals]], that do allow negative values. 
However, <math display="inline">p_K</math> might not be real-valued since for any given <math display="inline">x \in X,</math> the value <math display="inline">p_K(x)</math> is a real number if and only if <math display="inline">\{r > 0 : x \in r K\}</math> is not [[Empty set|empty]].
Consequently, <math display="inline">K</math> is usually assumed to have properties (such as being [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] in <math display="inline">X,</math> for instance) that will guarantee that <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued.

==Definition==

Let <math display="inline">K</math> be a subset of a real or complex vector space <math display="inline">X.</math> Define the {{em|gauge}} of <math display="inline">K</math> or the {{em|Minkowski functional}} associated with or induced by <math display="inline">K</math> as being the function <math display="inline">p_K : X \to [0, \infty],</math> valued in the [[Extended real number line|extended real number]]s, defined by

<math display=block>p_K(x) := \inf \{r > 0 : x \in r K\},</math>

(recall that the [[infimum]] of the empty set is <math display="inline">\,\infty</math>, that is, <math display="inline">\inf \varnothing = \infty</math>). Here, <math display="inline">\{r > 0 : x \in r K\}</math> is shorthand for <math display="inline">\{r \in \R : r > 0 \text{ and } x \in r K\}.</math>

For any <math display="inline">x \in X,</math> <math display="inline">p_K(x) \neq \infty</math> if and only if <math display="inline">\{r > 0 : x \in r K\}</math> is not empty. 
The arithmetic operations on <math display="inline">\R</math> [[Extended real number line#Arithmetic operations|can be extended]] to operate on <math display="inline">\pm \infty,</math> where <math display="inline">\frac{r}{\pm \infty} := 0</math> for all non-zero real <math display="inline">- \infty < r < \infty.</math> 
The products <math display="inline">0 \cdot \infty</math> and <math display="inline">0 \cdot - \infty</math> remain undefined.

===Some conditions making a gauge real-valued===

In the field of [[convex analysis]], the map <math display="inline">p_K</math> taking on the value of <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> is not necessarily an issue. 
However, in functional analysis <math display="inline">p_K</math> is almost always real-valued (that is, to never take on the value of <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math>), which happens if and only if the set <math display="inline">\{r > 0 : x \in r K\}</math> is non-empty for every <math display="inline">x \in X.</math>

In order for <math display="inline">p_K</math> to be real-valued, it suffices for the origin of <math display="inline">X</math> to belong to the {{em|[[algebraic interior]]}} or {{em|core}} of <math display="inline">K</math> in <math display="inline">X.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=109}} 
If <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] in <math display="inline">X,</math> where recall that this implies that <math display="inline">0 \in K,</math> then the origin belongs to the [[algebraic interior]] of <math display="inline">K</math> in <math display="inline">X</math> and thus <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued. 
Characterizations of when <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued are given below.

==Motivating examples==

===Example 1===

Consider a [[normed vector space]] <math display="inline">(X, \|\,\cdot\,\|),</math> with the norm <math display="inline">\|\,\cdot\,\|</math> and let <math display="inline">U := \{x\in X : \|x\| \leq 1\}</math> be the unit ball in <math display="inline">X.</math> Then for every <math display="inline">x \in X,</math> <math display="inline">\|x\| = p_U(x).</math> Thus the Minkowski functional <math display="inline">p_U</math> is just the norm on <math display="inline">X.</math>

===Example 2===

Let <math display="inline">X</math> be a vector space without topology with underlying scalar field <math display="inline">\mathbb{K}.</math>
Let <math display="inline">f : X \to \mathbb{K}</math> be any [[Linear form|linear functional]] on <math display="inline">X</math> (not necessarily continuous). 
Fix <math display="inline">a > 0.</math> 
Let <math display="inline">K</math> be the set 
<math display=block>K := \{x \in X : |f(x)| \leq a\}</math>
and let <math display="inline">p_K</math> be the Minkowski functional of <math display="inline">K.</math> 
Then
<math display=block>p_K(x) = \frac{1}{a} |f(x)| \quad \text{ for all } x \in X.</math>
The function <math display="inline">p_K</math> has the following properties:

#It is {{em|subadditive}}: <math display="inline">p_K(x + y) \leq p_K(x) + p_K(y).</math>
#It is {{em|absolutely homogeneous}}: <math display="inline">p_K(s x) = |s| p_K(x)</math> for all scalars <math display="inline">s.</math>
#It is {{em|nonnegative}}: <math display="inline">p_K \geq 0.</math>

Therefore, <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[seminorm]] on <math display="inline">X,</math> with an induced topology. 
This is characteristic of Minkowski functionals defined via "nice" sets. 
There is a one-to-one correspondence between seminorms and the Minkowski functional given by such sets. 
What is meant precisely by "nice" is discussed in the section below.

Notice that, in contrast to a stronger requirement for a norm, <math display="inline">p_K(x) = 0</math> need not imply <math display="inline">x = 0.</math> 
In the above example, one can take a nonzero <math display="inline">x</math> from the kernel of <math display="inline">f.</math> 
Consequently, the resulting topology need not be [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]].

==Common conditions guaranteeing gauges are seminorms==

To guarantee that <math display="inline">p_K(0) = 0,</math> it will henceforth be assumed that <math display="inline">0 \in K.</math>

In order for <math display="inline">p_K</math> to be a seminorm, it suffices for <math display="inline">K</math> to be a [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] (that is, convex and balanced) and absorbing in <math display="inline">X,</math> which are the most common assumption placed on <math display="inline">K.</math>

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=119}}|math_statement=
If <math display="inline">K</math> is an [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] in a vector space <math display="inline">X</math> then the Minkowski functional of <math display="inline">K,</math> which is the map <math display="inline">p_K : X \to [0, \infty)</math> defined by
<math display=block>p_K(x) := \inf \{r > 0 : x \in r K\},</math>
is a seminorm on <math display="inline">X.</math>
Moreover,
<math display=block>p_K(x) = \frac{1}{\sup \{r > 0 : r x \in K\}}.</math>
}}

More generally, if <math display="inline">K</math> is convex and the origin belongs to the [[algebraic interior]] of <math display="inline">K,</math> then <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a nonnegative [[sublinear functional]] on <math display="inline">X,</math> which implies in particular that it is [[subadditive]] and [[Positive homogeneity|positive homogeneous]].
If <math display="inline">K</math> is absorbing in <math display="inline">X</math> then <math display="inline">p_{[0, 1] K}</math> is positive homogeneous, meaning that <math display="inline">p_{[0, 1] K}(s x) = s p_{[0, 1] K}(x)</math> for all real <math display="inline">s \geq 0,</math> where <math display="inline">[0, 1] K = \{t k : t \in [0, 1], k \in K\}.</math>{{sfn|Jarchow|1981|pp=104-108}}
If <math display="inline">q</math> is a nonnegative real-valued function on <math display="inline">X</math> that is positive homogeneous, then the sets <math display="inline">U := \{x \in X : q(x) < 1\}</math> and <math display="inline">D := \{x \in X : q(x) \leq 1\}</math> satisfy <math display="inline">[0, 1] U = U</math> and <math display="inline">[0, 1] D = D;</math> 
if in addition <math display="inline">q</math> is absolutely homogeneous then both <math display="inline">U</math> and <math display="inline">D</math> are [[Balanced set|balanced]].{{sfn|Jarchow|1981|pp=104-108}}

===Gauges of absorbing disks===

Arguably the most common requirements placed on a set <math display="inline">K</math> to guarantee that <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a seminorm are that <math display="inline">K</math> be an [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] in <math display="inline">X.</math>
Due to how common these assumptions are, the properties of a Minkowski functional <math display="inline">p_K</math> when <math display="inline">K</math> is an absorbing disk will now be investigated. 
Since all of the results mentioned above made few (if any) assumptions on <math display="inline">K,</math> they can be applied in this special case.

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|math_statement=
Assume that <math display="inline">K</math> is an absorbing subset of <math display="inline">X.</math>
It is shown that: 
# If <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Convex set|convex]] then <math display="inline">p_K</math> is subadditive.
# If <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Balanced set|balanced]] then <math display="inline">p_K</math> is [[Homogeneous function|absolutely homogeneous]]; that is, <math display="inline">p_K(s x) = |s| p_K(x)</math> for all scalars <math display="inline">s.</math>
}}

{{collapse top|title=Proof that the Gauge of an absorbing disk is a seminorm|left=true}}
'''Convexity and subadditivity'''

A simple geometric argument that shows convexity of <math display="inline">K</math> implies subadditivity is as follows. 
Suppose for the moment that <math display="inline">p_K(x) = p_K(y) = r.</math> 
Then for all <math display="inline">e > 0,</math> <math display="inline">x, y \in K_e := (r, e) K.</math> 
Since <math display="inline">K</math> is convex and <math display="inline">r + e \neq 0,</math> <math display="inline">K_e</math> is also convex. 
Therefore, <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2} x + \frac{1}{2} y \in K_e.</math> 
By definition of the Minkowski functional <math display="inline">p_K,</math> 
<math display=block>p_K\left(\frac{1}{2} x + \frac{1}{2} y\right) \leq r + e = \frac{1}{2} p_K(x) + \frac{1}{2} p_K(y) + e.</math>

But the left hand side is <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2} p_K(x + y),</math> so that 
<math display=block>p_K(x + y) \leq p_K(x) + p_K(y) + 2 e.</math>

Since <math display="inline">e > 0</math> was arbitrary, it follows that <math display="inline">p_K(x + y) \leq p_K(x) + p_K(y),</math> which is the desired inequality. 
The general case <math display="inline">p_K(x) > p_K(y)</math> is obtained after the obvious modification.

Convexity of <math display="inline">K,</math> together with the initial assumption that the set <math display="inline">\{r > 0 : x \in r K\}</math> is nonempty, implies that <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Absorbing set|absorbing]].

'''Balancedness and absolute homogeneity'''

Notice that <math display="inline">K</math> being balanced implies that
<math display=block>\lambda x \in r K \quad \mbox{if and only if} \quad x \in \frac{r}{|\lambda|} K.</math>

Therefore
<math display=block>p_K (\lambda x) = \inf \left\{r > 0 : \lambda x \in r K \right\} 
= \inf \left\{r > 0 : x \in \frac{r}{|\lambda|} K \right\}
= \inf \left\{|\lambda|\frac{r}{|\lambda|} > 0 : x \in \frac{r}{|\lambda|} K \right\}
= |\lambda| p_K(x).
</math>
{{collapse bottom}}

===Algebraic properties===

Let <math display="inline">X</math> be a real or complex vector space and let <math display="inline">K</math> be an absorbing disk in <math display="inline">X.</math>

*<math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[seminorm]] on <math display="inline">X.</math>
*<math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] on <math display="inline">X</math> if and only if <math display="inline">K</math> does not contain a non-trivial vector subspace.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=115-154}}
*<math display="inline">p_{s K} = \frac{1}{|s|} p_K</math> for any scalar <math display="inline">s \neq 0.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=115-154}}
*If <math display="inline">J</math> is an absorbing disk in <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">J \subseteq K</math> then <math display="inline">p_K \leq p_J.</math>
*If <math display="inline">K</math> is a set satisfying <math display="inline">\{x \in X : p(x) < 1\} \; \subseteq \; K \; \subseteq \; \{x \in X : p(x) \leq 1\}</math> then <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] in <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">p = p_K,</math> where <math display="inline">p_K</math> is the Minkowski functional associated with <math display="inline">K;</math> that is, it is the gauge of <math display="inline">K.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|1999|p=40}}
* In particular, if <math display="inline">K</math> is as above and <math display="inline">q</math> is any seminorm on <math display="inline">X,</math> then <math display="inline">q = p</math> if and only if <math display="inline">\{x \in X : q(x) < 1\} \; \subseteq \; K \; \subseteq \; \{x \in X : q(x) \leq 1\}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|1999|p=40}}
*If <math display="inline">x \in X</math> satisfies <math display="inline">p_K(x) < 1</math> then <math display="inline">x \in K.</math>

===Topological properties===

Assume that <math display="inline">X</math> is a (real or complex) [[topological vector space]] (not necessarily [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] or [[locally convex]]) and let <math display="inline">K</math> be an absorbing disk in <math display="inline">X.</math> Then

<math display=block>\operatorname{Int}_X K \; \subseteq \; \{x \in X : p_K(x) < 1\} \; \subseteq \; K \; \subseteq \; \{x \in X : p_K(x) \leq 1\} \; \subseteq \; \operatorname{Cl}_X K,</math>

where <math display="inline">\operatorname{Int}_X K</math> is the [[topological interior]] and <math display="inline">\operatorname{Cl}_X K</math> is the [[Closure (topology)|topological closure]] of <math display="inline">K</math> in <math display="inline">X.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=119-120}} 
Importantly, it was {{em|not}} assumed that <math display="inline">p_K</math> was continuous nor was it assumed that <math display="inline">K</math> had any topological properties.

Moreover, the Minkowski functional <math display="inline">p_K</math> is continuous if and only if <math display="inline">K</math> is a neighborhood of the origin in <math display="inline">X.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=119-120}} 
If <math display="inline">p_K</math> is continuous then{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=119-120}}
<math display=block>\operatorname{Int}_X K = \{x \in X : p_K(x) < 1\} \quad \text{ and } \quad \operatorname{Cl}_X K = \{x \in X : p_K(x) \leq 1\}.</math>

==Minimal requirements on the set==

This section will investigate the most general case of the gauge of {{em|any}} subset <math display="inline">K</math> of <math display="inline">X.</math> 
The more common special case where <math display="inline">K</math> is assumed to be an [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] in <math display="inline">X</math> was discussed above.

===Properties===

All results in this section may be applied to the case where <math display="inline">K</math> is an absorbing disk.

Throughout, <math display="inline">K</math> is any subset of <math display="inline">X.</math>

{{Math theorem|name=Summary|style=overflow:scroll|math_statement=
Suppose that <math display="inline">K</math> is a subset of a real or complex vector space <math display="inline">X.</math>

#'''[[Strict positive homogeneity]]''': <math display="inline">p_K(r x) = r p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|positive}} real <math display="inline">r > 0.</math>
#* '''[[Nonnegative homogeneity|Positive/Nonnegative homogeneity]]''': <math display="inline">p_K</math> is nonnegative homogeneous if and only if <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued.
#** A map <math display="inline">p</math> is called {{em|[[Nonnegative homogeneity|nonnegative homogeneous]]}}{{sfn|Kubrusly|2011|p=200}} if <math display="inline">p(r x) = r p(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|nonnegative}} real <math display="inline">r \geq 0.</math> Since <math display="inline">0 \cdot \infty</math> is undefined, a map that takes infinity as a value is not nonnegative homogeneous.
#'''Real-values''': <math display="inline">(0, \infty) K</math> is the set of all points on which <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real valued. So <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued if and only if <math display="inline">(0, \infty) K = X,</math> in which case <math display="inline">0 \in K.</math>
#* '''Value at <math display="inline">0</math>''': <math display="inline">p_K(0) \neq \infty</math> if and only if <math display="inline">0 \in K</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_K(0) = 0.</math>
#* '''[[Null space]]''': If <math display="inline">x \in X</math> then <math display="inline">p_K(x) = 0</math> if and only if <math display="inline">(0, \infty) x \subseteq (0, 1) K</math> if and only if there exists a divergent sequence of positive real numbers <math display="inline">t_1, t_2, t_3, \cdots \to \infty</math> such that <math display="inline">t_n x \in K</math> for all <math display="inline">n.</math> Moreover, the [[zero set]] of <math display="inline">p_K</math> is <math display="inline">\ker p_K ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \left\{y \in X : p_K(y) = 0 \right\} = {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, e) K.</math>
#'''Comparison to a constant''': If <math display="inline">0 \leq r \leq \infty</math> then for any <math display="inline">x \in X,</math> <math display="inline">p_K(x) < r</math> if and only if <math display="inline">x \in (0, r) K;</math> this can be restated as: If <math display="inline">0 \leq r \leq \infty</math> then <math display="inline">p_K^{-1}([0, r)) = (0, r) K.</math>
#* It follows that if <math display="inline">0 \leq R < \infty</math> is real then <math display="inline">p_K^{-1}([0, R]) = {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, R + e) K,</math> where the set on the right hand side denotes <math display="inline">{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} [(0, R + e) K]</math> and not its subset <math display="inline">\left[{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, R + e)\right] K = (0, R] K.</math> If <math display="inline">R > 0</math> then these sets are equal if and only if <math display="inline">K</math> contains <math display="inline">\left\{y \in X : p_K(y) = 1 \right\}.</math> 
#* In particular, if <math display="inline">x \in R K</math> or <math display="inline">x \in (0, R] K</math> then <math display="inline">p_K(x) \leq R,</math> but importantly, the converse is not necessarily true. <!--- Note that if <math display="inline">R = 0</math> then <math display="inline">(0, R] K = \varnothing</math> so <math display="inline">x \in (0, R] K</math> implies <math display="inline">R \neq 0.</math> --->
#'''Gauge comparison''': For any subset <math display="inline">L \subseteq X,</math> <math display="inline">p_K \leq p_L</math> if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) L \subseteq (0, 1) K;</math> thus <math display="inline">p_L = p_K</math> if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) L = (0, 1) K.</math> 
#* The assignment <math display="inline">L \mapsto p_L</math> is order-reversing in the sense that if <math display="inline">K \subseteq L</math> then <math display="inline">p_L \leq p_K.</math>{{sfn|Schechter|1996|p=316}}
#* Because the set <math display="inline">L := (0, 1) K</math> satisfies <math display="inline">(0, 1) L = (0, 1) K,</math> it follows that replacing <math display="inline">K</math> with <math display="inline">p_K^{-1}([0, 1)) = (0, 1) K</math> will not change the resulting Minkowski functional. The same is true of <math display="inline">L := (0, 1] K</math> and of <math display="inline">L := p_K^{-1}([0, 1]).</math>
#* If <math display="inline">D ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \left\{y \in X : p_K(y) = 1 \text{ or } p_K(y) = 0 \right\}</math> then <math display="inline">p_D = p_K</math> and <math display="inline">D</math> has the particularly nice property that if <math display="inline">r > 0</math> is real then <math display="inline">x \in r D</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_D(x) = r</math> or <math display="inline">p_D(x) = 0.</math><ref group=note>It is in general '''{{em|false}}''' that <math display="inline">x \in r D</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_D(x) = r</math> (for example, consider when <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] or a seminorm). The correct statement is: If <math display="inline">0 < r < \infty</math> then <math display="inline">x \in r D</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_D(x) = r</math> or <math display="inline">p_D(x) = 0.</math></ref> Moreover, if <math display="inline">r > 0</math> is real then <math display="inline">p_D(x) \leq r</math> if and only if <math display="inline">x \in (0, r] D.</math>
#'''[[Subadditive]]'''/'''Triangle inequality''': <math display="inline">p_K</math> is subadditive if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> is convex. If <math display="inline">K</math> is convex then so are both <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> and <math display="inline">(0, 1] K</math> and moreover, <math display="inline">p_K</math> is subadditive.
#'''Scaling the set''': If <math display="inline">s \neq 0</math> is a scalar then <math display="inline">p_{s K}(y) = p_K\left(\tfrac{1}{s} y\right)</math> for all <math display="inline">y \in X.</math> Thus if <math display="inline">0 < r < \infty</math> is real then <math display="inline">p_{r K}(y) = p_K\left(\tfrac{1}{r} y\right) = \tfrac{1}{r} p_K(y).</math>
#'''Symmetric''': <math display="inline">p_K</math> is symmetric (meaning that <math display="inline">p_K(- y) = p_K(y)</math> for all <math display="inline">y \in X</math>) if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> is a [[symmetric set]] (meaning that<math display="inline">(0, 1) K = - (0, 1) K</math>), which happens if and only if <math display="inline">p_K = p_{- K}.</math>
#'''[[Absolute homogeneity]]''': <math display="inline">p_K(u x) = p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all unit length scalars <math display="inline">u</math><ref group=note><math display="inline">u</math> is having unit length means that <math display="inline">|u| = 1.</math></ref> if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) u K \subseteq (0, 1) K</math> for all unit length scalars <math display="inline">u,</math> in which case <math display="inline">p_K(s x) = |s| p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|non-zero}} scalars <math display="inline">s \neq 0.</math> If in addition <math display="inline">p_K</math> is also real-valued then this holds for {{em|all}} scalars <math display="inline">s</math> (that is, <math display="inline">p_K</math> is absolutely homogeneous<ref group=note>The map <math display="inline">p_K</math> is called {{em|absolutely homogeneous}} if <math display="inline">|s| p_K(x)</math> is well-defined and <math display="inline">p_K(s x) = |s| p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all scalars <math display="inline">s</math> (not just non-zero scalars).</ref>).
#* <math display="inline">(0, 1) u K \subseteq (0, 1) K</math> for all unit length <math display="inline">u</math> if and only if <math display="inline">(0, 1) u K = (0, 1) K</math> for all unit length <math display="inline">u.</math>
#* <math display="inline">s K \subseteq K</math> for all unit scalars <math display="inline">s</math> if and only if <math display="inline">s K = K</math> for all unit scalars <math display="inline">s;</math> if this is the case then <math display="inline">(0, 1) K = (0, 1) s K</math> for all unit scalars <math display="inline">s.</math>
#* The Minkowski functional of any [[balanced set]] is a [[balanced function]].{{sfn|Schechter|1996|p=316}} 
#'''[[Absorbing set|Absorbing]]''': If <math display="inline">K</math> is convex {{em|or}} balanced and if <math display="inline">(0, \infty) K = X</math> then <math display="inline">K</math> is absorbing in <math display="inline">X.</math>
#* If a set <math display="inline">A</math> is absorbing in <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">A \subseteq K</math> then <math display="inline">K</math> is absorbing in <math display="inline">X.</math>
#* If <math display="inline">K</math> is convex and <math display="inline">0 \in K</math> then <math display="inline">[0, 1] K = K,</math> in which case <math display="inline">(0, 1) K \subseteq K.</math>
#'''Restriction to a vector subspace''': If <math display="inline">S</math> is a vector subspace of <math display="inline">X</math> and if <math display="inline">p_{K \cap S} : S \to [0, \infty]</math> denotes the Minkowski functional of <math display="inline">K \cap S</math> on <math display="inline">S,</math> then <math display="inline">p_K\big\vert_S = p_{K \cap S},</math> where <math display="inline">p_K\big\vert_S</math> denotes the [[Restriction of a function|restriction]] of <math display="inline">p_K</math> to <math display="inline">S.</math>
}}

{{collapse top|title=Proof|left=true}}
The proofs of these basic properties are straightforward exercises so only the proofs of the most important statements are given.

The proof that a convex subset <math display="inline">A \subseteq X</math> that satisfies <math display="inline">(0, \infty) A = X</math> is necessarily [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] in <math display="inline">X</math> is straightforward and can be found in the article on [[absorbing set]]s.

For any real <math display="inline">t > 0,</math>

<math display=block>\{r > 0 : t x \in r K\} = \{t(r/t) : x \in (r/t) K\} = t \{s > 0 : x \in s K\}</math>

so that taking the infimum of both sides shows that

<math display=block>p_K(tx) = \inf \{r > 0 : t x \in r K\} = t \inf \{s > 0 : x \in s K\} = t p_K(x).</math>

This proves that Minkowski functionals are strictly positive homogeneous. For <math display="inline">0 \cdot p_K(x)</math> to be well-defined, it is necessary and sufficient that <math display="inline">p_K(x) \neq \infty;</math> thus <math display="inline">p_K(tx) = t p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|non-negative}} real <math display="inline">t \geq 0</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued.

The hypothesis of statement (7) allows us to conclude that <math display="inline">p_K(s x) = p_K(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all scalars <math display="inline">s</math> satisfying <math display="inline">|s| = 1.</math> 
Every scalar <math display="inline">s</math> is of the form <math display="inline">r e^{i t}</math> for some real <math display="inline">t</math> where <math display="inline">r := |s| \geq 0</math> and <math display="inline">e^{i t}</math> is real if and only if <math display="inline">s</math> is real. 
The results in the statement about absolute homogeneity follow immediately from the aforementioned conclusion, from the strict positive homogeneity of <math display="inline">p_K,</math> and from the positive homogeneity of <math display="inline">p_K</math> when <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued. 
<math display="inline">\blacksquare</math>
{{collapse bottom}}

===Examples===

#If <math display="inline">\mathcal{L}</math> is a non-empty collection of subsets of <math display="inline">X</math> then <math display="inline">p_{\cup \mathcal{L}}(x) = \inf \left\{p_L(x) : L \in \mathcal{L} \right\}</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X,</math> where <math display="inline">\cup \mathcal{L} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ {\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{L \in \mathcal{L}}} L.</math> 
#* Thus <math display="inline">p_{K \cup L}(x) = \min \left\{p_K(x), p_L(x) \right\}</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X.</math> 
#If <math display="inline">\mathcal{L}</math> is a non-empty collection of subsets of <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">I \subseteq X</math> satisfies 
<math display=block>\left\{x \in X : p_L(x) < 1 \text{ for all } L \in \mathcal{L}\right\} \quad \subseteq \quad I \quad \subseteq \quad \left\{x \in X : p_L(x) \leq 1 \text{ for all } L \in \mathcal{L}\right\}</math> 
then <math display="inline">p_I(x) = \sup \left\{p_L(x) : L \in \mathcal{L}\right\}</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X.</math>

The following examples show that the containment <math display="inline">(0, R] K \; \subseteq \; {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, R + e) K</math> could be proper.

'''Example''': If <math display="inline">R = 0</math> and <math display="inline">K = X</math> then <math display="inline">(0, R] K = (0, 0] X = \varnothing X = \varnothing</math> but <math display="inline">{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, e) K = {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} X = X,</math> which shows that its possible for <math display="inline">(0, R] K</math> to be a proper subset of <math display="inline">{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, R + e) K</math> when <math display="inline">R = 0.</math> <math display="inline">\blacksquare</math>

The next example shows that the containment can be proper when <math display="inline">R = 1;</math> the example may be generalized to any real <math display="inline">R > 0.</math> 
Assuming that <math display="inline">[0, 1] K \subseteq K,</math> the following example is representative of how it happens that <math display="inline">x \in X</math> satisfies <math display="inline">p_K(x) = 1</math> but <math display="inline">x \not\in (0, 1] K.</math>

'''Example''': Let <math display="inline">x \in X</math> be non-zero and let <math display="inline">K = [0, 1) x</math> so that <math display="inline">[0, 1] K = K</math> and <math display="inline">x \not\in K.</math> 
From <math display="inline">x \not\in (0, 1) K = K</math> it follows that <math display="inline">p_K(x) \geq 1.</math> 
That <math display="inline">p_K(x) \leq 1</math> follows from observing that for every <math display="inline">e > 0,</math> <math display="inline">(0, 1 + e) K = [0, 1 + e)([0, 1) x) = [0, 1 + e) x,</math> which contains <math display="inline">x.</math> 
Thus <math display="inline">p_K(x) = 1</math> and <math display="inline">x \in {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{e > 0}} (0, 1 + e) K.</math> 
However, <math display="inline">(0, 1] K = (0, 1]([0, 1) x) = [0, 1) x = K</math> so that <math display="inline">x \not\in (0, 1] K,</math> as desired. 
<math display="inline">\blacksquare</math>

===Positive homogeneity characterizes Minkowski functionals===

The next theorem shows that Minkowski functionals are {{em|exactly}} those functions <math display="inline">f : X \to [0, \infty]</math> that have a certain purely algebraic property that is commonly encountered.

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|math_statement=
Let <math display="inline">f : X \to [0, \infty]</math> be any function. 
The following statements are equivalent:

#'''[[Strict positive homogeneity]]''': <math display="inline">\; f(t x) = t f(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|positive}} real <math display="inline">t > 0.</math>
#* This statement is equivalent to: <math display="inline">f(t x) \leq t f(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all positive real <math display="inline">t > 0.</math>
#<math display="inline">f</math> is a Minkowski functional: meaning that there exists a subset <math display="inline">S \subseteq X</math> such that <math display="inline">f = p_S.</math>
#<math display="inline">f = p_K</math> where <math display="inline">K := \{x \in X : f(x) \leq 1\}.</math>
#<math display="inline">f = p_V \,</math> where <math display="inline">V \,:= \{x \in X : f(x) < 1\}.</math>

Moreover, if <math display="inline">f</math> never takes on the value <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> (so that the product <math display="inline">0 \cdot f(x)</math> is always well-defined) then this list may be extended to include: 
{{ordered list|start=5
|'''[[Positive homogeneity|Positive]]'''/'''[[Nonnegative homogeneity]]''': <math display="inline">f(t x) = t f(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all {{em|nonnegative}} real <math display="inline">t \geq 0</math>.
}}
}}

{{collapse top|title=Proof|left=true}}
If <math display="inline">f(t x) \leq t f(x)</math> holds for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and real <math display="inline">t > 0</math> then <math display="inline">t f(x) = t f\left(\tfrac{1}{t}(t x)\right) \leq t \tfrac{1}{t} f(t x) = f(t x) \leq t f(x)</math> so that <math display="inline">t f(x) = f(t x).</math>

Only (1) implies (3) will be proven because afterwards, the rest of the theorem follows immediately from the basic properties of Minkowski functionals described earlier; properties that will henceforth be used without comment. 
So assume that <math display="inline">f : X \to [0, \infty]</math> is a function such that <math display="inline">f(t x) = t f(x)</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math> and all real <math display="inline">t > 0</math> and let <math display="inline">K := \{y \in X : f(y) \leq 1\}.</math> 
<!--- START: Unnecessary extra details: ----
Note that if <math display="inline">z \in X</math> is such that <math display="inline">f(z) \neq \infty</math> then either <math display="inline">z \in K</math> or else <math display="inline">f(z) > 1</math> and <math display="inline">\tfrac{1}{f(z)} z \in K</math> so that either way, some positive real scalar multiple of <math display="inline">z</math> will belong to <math display="inline">K.</math> 
Similarly, if <math display="inline">z \in X</math> is such that <math display="inline">f(z) \neq 0</math> then some positive real scalar multiple of <math display="inline">z</math> will {{em|not}} belong to <math display="inline">K.</math> 
It follows that <math display="inline">f</math> is identically <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> (resp. identically <math display="inline">0</math>) if and only if <math display="inline">K = \varnothing</math> (resp. <math display="inline">K = X</math>), which happens if and only if <math display="inline">p_K</math> is identically <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> (resp. identically <math display="inline">0</math>). 
So henceforth assume that <math display="inline">K</math> is neither empty nor all of <math display="inline">X</math> and that <math display="inline">f</math> is neither identically <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> nor identically <math display="inline">0.</math> 
--- END ----->

For all real <math display="inline">t > 0,</math> <math display="inline">f(0) = f(t 0) = t f(0)</math> so by taking <math display="inline">t = 2</math> for instance, it follows that either <math display="inline">f(0) = 0</math> or <math display="inline">f(0) = \infty.</math> 
Let <math display="inline">x \in X.</math> 
It remains to show that <math display="inline">f(x) = p_K(x).</math>

It will now be shown that if <math display="inline">f(x) = 0</math> or <math display="inline">f(x) = \infty</math> then <math display="inline">f(x) = p_K(x),</math> so that in particular, it will follow that <math display="inline">f(0) = p_K(0).</math> 
So suppose that <math display="inline">f(x) = 0</math> or <math display="inline">f(x) = \infty;</math> in either case <math display="inline">f(t x) = t f(x) = f(x)</math> for all real <math display="inline">t > 0.</math> 
Now if <math display="inline">f(x) = 0</math> then this implies that that <math display="inline">t x \in K</math> for all real <math display="inline">t > 0</math> (since <math display="inline">f(t x) = 0 \leq 1</math>), which implies that <math display="inline">p_K(x) = 0,</math> as desired. 
Similarly, if <math display="inline">f(x) = \infty</math> then <math display="inline">t x \not\in K</math> for all real <math display="inline">t > 0,</math> which implies that <math display="inline">p_K(x) = \infty,</math> as desired. 
Thus, it will henceforth be assumed that <math display="inline">R := f(x)</math> a positive real number and that <math display="inline">x \neq 0</math> (importantly, however, the possibility that <math display="inline">p_K(x)</math> is <math display="inline">0</math> or <math display="inline">\,\infty\,</math> has not yet been ruled out).

Recall that just like <math display="inline">f,</math> the function <math display="inline">p_K</math> satisfies <math display="inline">p_K(t x) = t p_K(x)</math> for all real <math display="inline">t > 0.</math> 
Since <math display="inline">0 < \tfrac{1}{R} < \infty,</math> <math display="inline">p_K(x)= R = f(x)</math> if and only if <math display="inline">p_K\left(\tfrac{1}{R} x\right) = 1 = f\left(\tfrac{1}{R} x\right)</math> so assume without loss of generality that <math display="inline">R = 1</math> and it remains to show that <math display="inline">p_K\left(\tfrac{1}{R} x\right) = 1.</math> 
Since <math display="inline">f(x) = 1,</math> <math display="inline">x \in K \subseteq (0, 1] K,</math> which implies that <math display="inline">p_K(x) \leq 1</math> (so in particular, <math display="inline">p_K(x) \neq \infty</math> is guaranteed). 
It remains to show that <math display="inline">p_K(x) \geq 1,</math> which recall happens if and only if <math display="inline">x \not\in (0, 1) K.</math> 
So assume for the sake of contradiction that <math display="inline">x \in (0, 1) K</math> and let <math display="inline">0 < r < 1</math> and <math display="inline">k \in K</math> be such that <math display="inline">x = r k,</math> where note that <math display="inline">k \in K</math> implies that <math display="inline">f(k) \leq 1.</math> 
Then <math display="inline">1 = f(x) = f(r k) = r f(k) \leq r < 1.</math> <math display="inline">\blacksquare</math>
{{collapse bottom}}

This theorem can be extended to characterize certain classes of <math display="inline">[- \infty, \infty]</math>-valued maps (for example, real-valued [[sublinear function]]s) in terms of Minkowski functionals. 
For instance, it can be used to describe how every real homogeneous function <math display="inline">f : X \to \R</math> (such as linear functionals) can be written in terms of a unique Minkowski functional having a certain property.

===Characterizing Minkowski functionals on star sets===

{{Math theorem|name=Proposition{{sfn|Schechter|1996|pp=313-317}}|style=overflow:scroll|math_statement=
Let <math display="inline">f : X \to [0, \infty]</math> be any function and <math display="inline">K \subseteq X</math> be any subset. 
The following statements are equivalent:

#<math display="inline">f</math> is (strictly) positive homogeneous, <math display="inline">f(0) = 0,</math> and <p><math display=block>\{x \in X : f(x) < 1\} \; \subseteq \; K \; \subseteq \; \{x \in X : f(x) \leq 1\}.</math></p>
#<math display="inline">f</math> is the Minkowski functional of <math display="inline">K</math> (that is, <math display="inline">f = p_K</math>), <math display="inline">K</math> contains the origin, and <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Star domain|star-shaped]] at the origin.
#* The set <math display="inline">K</math> is star-shaped at the origin if and only if <math display="inline">t k \in K</math> whenever <math display="inline">k \in K</math> and <math display="inline">0 \leq t \leq 1.</math> A set that is star-shaped at the origin is sometimes called a {{em|star set}}.{{sfn|Schechter|1996|p=303}}
}}

===Characterizing Minkowski functionals that are seminorms===

In this next theorem, which follows immediately from the statements above, <math display="inline">K</math> is {{em|not}} assumed to be absorbing in <math display="inline">X</math> and instead, it is deduced that <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> is absorbing when <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a seminorm. It is also not assumed that <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Balanced set|balanced]] (which is a property that <math display="inline">K</math> is often required to have); in its place is the weaker condition that <math display="inline">(0, 1) s K \subseteq (0, 1) K</math> for all scalars <math display="inline">s</math> satisfying <math display="inline">|s| = 1.</math> 
The common requirement that <math display="inline">K</math> be convex is also weakened to only requiring that <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> be convex.

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|math_statement=
Let <math display="inline">K</math> be a subset of a real or complex vector space <math display="inline">X.</math> 
Then <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[seminorm]] on <math display="inline">X</math> if and only if all of the following conditions hold:

#<math display="inline">(0, \infty) K = X</math> (or equivalently, <math display="inline">p_K</math> is real-valued).
#<math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> is convex (or equivalently, <math display="inline">p_K</math> is [[subadditivity|subadditive]]).
#* It suffices (but is not necessary) for <math display="inline">K</math> to be convex.
#<math display="inline">(0, 1) u K \subseteq (0, 1) K</math> for all unit scalars <math display="inline">u.</math>
#* This condition is satisfied if <math display="inline">K</math> is [[Balanced set|balanced]] or more generally if <math display="inline">u K \subseteq K</math> for all unit scalars <math display="inline">u.</math>

in which case <math display="inline">0 \in K</math> and both <math display="inline">(0, 1) K = \{x \in X : p(x) < 1\}</math> and <math display="inline">\bigcap_{e > 0} (0, 1 + e) K = \left\{x \in X : p_K(x) \leq 1\right\}</math> will be convex, balanced, and [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] subsets of <math display="inline">X.</math>

Conversely, if <math display="inline">f</math> is a seminorm on <math display="inline">X</math> then the set <math display="inline">V := \{x \in X : f(x) < 1\}</math> satisfies all three of the above conditions (and thus also the conclusions) and also <math display="inline">f = p_V;</math> 
moreover, <math display="inline">V</math> is necessarily convex, balanced, absorbing, and satisfies <math display="inline">(0, 1) V = V = [0, 1] V.</math> 
}}

{{Math theorem|name=Corollary|math_statement=
If <math display="inline">K</math> is a convex, balanced, and absorbing subset of a real or complex vector space <math display="inline">X,</math> then <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a [[seminorm]] on <math display="inline">X.</math> 
}}

===Positive sublinear functions and Minkowski functionals===

It may be shown that a real-valued [[subadditive function]] <math display="inline">f : X \to \R</math> on an arbitrary [[topological vector space]] <math display="inline">X</math> is continuous at the origin if and only if it is uniformly continuous, where if in addition <math display="inline">f</math> is nonnegative, then <math display="inline">f</math> is continuous if and only if <math display="inline">V := \{x \in X : f(x) < 1\}</math> is an open neighborhood in <math display="inline">X.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=192-193}} 
If <math display="inline">f : X \to \R</math> is subadditive and satisfies <math display="inline">f(0) = 0,</math> then <math display="inline">f</math> is continuous if and only if its absolute value <math display="inline">|f| : X \to [0, \infty)</math> is continuous.

A {{em|nonnegative [[sublinear function]]}} is a [[Nonnegative homogeneity|nonnegative homogeneous]] function <math display="inline">f : X \to [0, \infty)</math> that satisfies the triangle inequality. 
It follows immediately from the results below that for such a function <math display="inline">f,</math> if <math display="inline">V := \{x \in X : f(x) < 1\}</math> then <math display="inline">f = p_V.</math> 
Given <math display="inline">K \subseteq X,</math> the Minkowski functional <math display="inline">p_K</math> is a sublinear function if and only if it is real-valued and subadditive, which is happens if and only if <math display="inline">(0, \infty) K = X</math> and <math display="inline">(0, 1) K</math> is convex.

===Correspondence between open convex sets and positive continuous sublinear functions===

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=192–193}}|style=overflow:scroll|math_statement=
Suppose that <math display="inline">X</math> is a [[topological vector space]] (not necessarily [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] or Hausdorff) over the real or complex numbers. 
Then the non-empty open convex subsets of <math display="inline">X</math> are exactly those sets that are of the form <math display="inline">z + \{x \in X : p(x) < 1\} = \{x \in X : p(x - z) < 1\}</math> for some <math display="inline">z \in X</math> and some positive continuous [[sublinear function]] <math display="inline">p</math> on <math display="inline">X.</math>
}}

{{collapse top|title=Proof|left=true}}
Let <math display="inline">V \neq \varnothing</math> be an open convex subset of <math display="inline">X.</math> 
If <math display="inline">0 \in V</math> then let <math display="inline">z := 0</math> and otherwise let <math display="inline">z \in V</math> be arbitrary. 
Let <math display="inline">p = p_K : X \to [0, \infty)</math> be the Minkowski functional of <math display="inline">K := V - z</math> where this convex open neighborhood of the origin satisfies <math display="inline">(0, 1) K = K.</math> 
Then <math display="inline">p</math> is a continuous sublinear function on <math display="inline">X</math> since <math display="inline">V - z</math> is convex, absorbing, and open (however, <math display="inline">p</math> is not necessarily a seminorm since it is not necessarily absolutely homogeneous). 
From the properties of Minkowski functionals, we have <math display="inline">p_K^{-1}([0, 1)) = (0, 1) K,</math> from which it follows that <math display="inline">V - z = \{x \in X : p(x) < 1\}</math> and so 
<math display="inline">V = z + \{x \in X : p(x) < 1\}.</math> 
Since <math display="inline">z + \{x \in X : p(x) < 1\} = \{x \in X : p(x - z) < 1\},</math> this completes the proof. <math display="inline">\blacksquare</math>
{{collapse bottom}}
